newsitem.title: BARBADOS: Caribbean leaders happier after Clinton summit.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean leaders happier after Clinton summit.

text.p: Leaders of the 14-member Caribbean Community, Haiti and the Dominican Republic emerged from their summit meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton saying future relations looked far rosier than they had going into the meeting.
Jamaica's Prime Minister P.J. Patterson, who chaired the summit, said participants had "agreed to chart a course that will enable us to move forward and together in the days ahead."
Regional officials said Clinton was expected soon to name a special White House liaison for Caribbean affairs to serve as Clinton's point man in the region.

In addition, there will be annual meetings of the region's foreign ministers with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, as well as continued efforts by the working groups that laid the ground work for the summit.

The leaders on Saturday signed a 30-page declaration and plan of action covering a wide range of trade and security issues, as well as pledges to cooperate in areas such as education, disaster preparedness and telecommunications.

Going into the summit, the general consensus was that U.S.- Caribbean relations were at their lowest ebb in decades, but the two hours of talks and a working lunch resulted in agreements on a number of issues vexing the region.

The new collaborative mechanisms addressed Caribbean concerns that the United States was too quick to take unilateral action in areas such as its controversial "certification" of other nations' anti-narcotics programs.
"If we are to be engaged in partnership", Patterson said, "a process of collective evaluation and decision-making" was required. He expressed satisfaction that such a mechanism was now in place.
Also encouraging, he said, was Clinton's assurance that he was "fully supporting" the Caribbean's request for an expansion of the Caribbean Basin Initiative on trade.

Regional leaders had requested the initiative be upgraded to provide parity with the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) between the United States, Mexico and Canada, and that this serve as a transitional mechanism to take the Caribbean into any future Americas-wide free trade zone.
Clinton said he planned to make a bill on that issue part of his budget presentation, although he conceded it would likely face opposition in Congress.

The region was also confident it had started a dialogue with Washington on U.S. policy toward Cuba. The region fears recent attempts to tighten the U.S. embargo against Cuba will lead to political instability, which could dry up investment in the region needed to replace dwindling aid flows.
"We said we would be prepared to give any assistance that we could in helping the U.S. normalize relations with Cuba," said St. Vincent Prime Minister Sir James Mitchell.
He added Clinton was "very firm" there would have to be substantial changes in Cuba before relations could resume.

The only remaining sore point was the continued U.S. effort to bring an end to the region's preferential banana export regime with the European Union. The Caribbean accounts for 15 percent of the total EU banana market, and the industry brings in $250-300 million a year in earnings.

In several countries, including St. Vincent, bananas account for 70 percent or more of total export earnings. Mitchell said he was "disappointed" that the United States still insisted that a recent World Trade Organization ruling against the EU regime be implemented.

The region had asked Clinton to hold off on implementing the ruling until 2002, when the regime is set to expire. Clinton did not give any assurances, and Mitchell observed "it would be a bit much to get him to go all the way on that at this stage."

The prime minister said the Caribbean was satisfied it "got the message across" that there had to be a gradual transition away from dependence on bananas, in order to avoid possible economic dislocation that could strengthen the hand of drug traffickers in the region.

The United States has agreed to finance programs to diversify the economies of the banana-dependent countries, and to meet in Brussels with the EU and the Caribbean to find a mutually acceptable compromise on the banana issue.
